name: NJ-12
label: Safe D

key_factors: District's D+13 partisan lean in a reliably Democratic New Jersey seat
Lopsided money race: Hamawy has $1.5M raised plus $1.9M outside support versus Mele's $79K
Prediction markets price Democrats at roughly 96 percent to hold the seat
Open seat removes incumbency benefits but no evidence of a competitive Republican operation
model.rationale: The district's D+13 lean, a massive financial advantage for Adam Hamawy in candidate and outside spending, and prediction markets pricing Democrats near 96 percent all point to a comfortable Democratic hold despite the open seat created by Bonnie Watson Coleman's retirement.
model.watch: Any late polling or unexpected outside spending against Hamawy, or an unusually strong Republican environment in New Jersey, could narrow the margin.
notes: No expert rater lists this race; treated as safe for the party holding the seat.
No usable general-election polls; forecast rests on fundamentals and expert ratings.
Open seat: Bonnie Watson Coleman (D) is not on the ballot.

overview:
New Jersey's 12th District in the central part of the state has a Democratic partisan lean of about 13 points, and Democrats have held it comfortably for years. With Bonnie Watson Coleman retiring, Democrat Adam Hamawy and Republican Gregg Mele lead the field. Hamawy has raised roughly $1.5 million and benefits from about $1.9 million in outside support, while Mele has raised under $100,000 with minimal cash on hand. Prediction markets give Democrats roughly a 96 percent chance of keeping the seat.

No public general-election polling covers this race, so the forecast rests on the district's partisan baseline and the stark resource gap between the candidates. The wide expected margin and moderate uncertainty reflect a reliably blue open seat with little evidence of a serious Republican campaign operation.
